analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal sugar price support program that keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in a House Agriculture subcommittee, and sugar growers kept their price support program for another three decades.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the federal sugar price support program, starting with the 1990 crop of sugar beets and sugarcane [S2][S3]. The program guarantees growers a minimum price for sugar, which keeps U.S. sugar prices well above the world price; those higher prices are paid by every household and food company that buys sugar. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its sugar subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, who currently pay more for sugar and for products made with it — candy, soft drinks, baked goods, cereal — than they would at world prices. Food and beverage manufacturers would pay less for their main sweetener. Taxpayers also benefit in years when sugar growers default on government price-support loans and the Treasury takes the loss, a risk the bill would eliminate.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sugar price support program under the Agricultural Act of 1949, effective for the 1990 crop of sugar beets and sugarcane, striking the provisions that guarantee growers a minimum price [S2][S3].

Because the program works by keeping domestic sugar prices above the world price, ending it would lower the price of sugar and of the thousands of grocery products made with it, a saving spread across every household that buys food rather than to any one group (general knowledge about how the program works; the repeal itself is in [S3]).

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers, and the processors who mill their crop, would see their guaranteed prices disappear and their revenue fall toward lower world prices. Workers and rural communities in sugar-producing regions — Florida, Louisiana, Hawaii, and the beet-growing Upper Midwest — would bear job losses and lower farm incomes.

drawbacks.text: Growers and sugar-region workers would bear real costs: without the guaranteed price, sugar would sell at world levels that have often been below U.S. production costs, cutting farm incomes and threatening sugar mill and refinery jobs [S3].

A good-faith objection is that the U.S. would be dismantling its support unilaterally while foreign governments subsidize their own sugar industries, potentially shifting production and jobs overseas rather than lowering prices as much as supporters hope (a widely made argument; the bill's unilateral repeal is in [S3]).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are spread thin but wide: a small saving per household on groceries and a lower risk of taxpayer losses on farm loans. The costs are concentrated and severe for a few thousand sugar farms and the towns that depend on them. That asymmetry is exactly why the program has survived — its beneficiaries fight hard for it while its payers, every grocery shopper, have no reason to organize. The bill was a clean repeal with no transition aid for growers, so some hardship in sugar regions would have been unavoidable.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its sugar subcommittee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Porter introduced the bill on May 17, 1989, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee the same day, and five days later to the Subcommittee on Cotton, Rice, and Sugar [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors, who kept a program that guarantees them prices above the world level, with the higher cost continuing to be paid by every household and food company that buys sugar.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers kept their price supports

for.name: Rep. John Edward Porter
for.role: Sole sponsor of the repeal bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the sugar price support program on May 17, 1989.

against.name: Subcommittee on Cotton, Rice, and Sugar of the House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee subpanel with jurisdiction over sugar policy
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 22, 1989 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after the referral; it remained in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors
against.role: Beneficiaries of the sugar price support program
against.what_they_did: Worked to preserve the sugar program, one of the longest-standing agricultural price supports, which survived repeated repeal attempts in this era.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors
industries.note: The bill would have ended their guaranteed minimum price, which is financed by the difference between high U.S. sugar prices and lower world prices — a cost paid by consumers. Their interest in keeping the program runs directly against shoppers' interest in cheaper sugar [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers (candy, soft drinks, baked goods)
industries.note: Sugar is a major input cost for these industries, and the price support program makes them pay above-world prices; repeal would cut their costs. Their savings would pass to consumers only through competition, but their interest in cheaper sugar runs alongside shoppers'.
The support program uses government loans against sugar crops; when prices fall, growers can forfeit their crop and leave the Treasury with the loss. Repeal would end that taxpayer exposure [S3].
